content:
The CAT (Comprehensive Attention Test) is a standardized assessment that measures multiple sub-domains of attention in a multidimensional way, taking into account developmental characteristics and situational context across age groups. Beyond simply determining whether someone “focuses well or poorly,” it provides objective scores for selective attention, sustained attention, divided attention, working memory, and inhibitory control.
It is widely used to assess cognitive difficulties associated with ADHD, academic underperformance, impulse control problems, anxiety, and depression. The CAT can be administered across a broad age range — from children and adolescents to adults. It provides an attention profile with percentile ranks and standard scores based on age-group norms, and identifies specific strengths and weaknesses across sub-domains such as visual vs. auditory and selective vs. sustained attention. It also serves as a foundational data source for evaluating clinical difficulties such as ADHD, learning disabilities, impulse control disorders, and depressive/anxiety disorders, and for designing personalized interventions including cognitive training, neurofeedback, and psychotherapy.
Age Ranges and Subtests The CAT uses different tasks suited to each age group. Game-format tasks are provided according to the developmental level of the examinee, with difficulty and stimulus type varying by age.
Early Childhood & Children (Ages 4 – Lower Elementary)
Visual Selective Attention: Quickly and accurately locating target stimuli among multiple images Auditory Selective Attention: Distinguishing and responding to specific sounds Sustained Attention: Maintaining consistent attention when the same stimulus is repeated Working Memory & Inhibitory Control: Remembering previously presented rules and avoiding impulsive responses Adolescents (Upper Elementary – High School)
Visual/Auditory Sustained Attention: Maintaining attention over extended periods Divided Attention: Responding simultaneously to two types of stimuli (e.g., sound + image) Shifting Attention: Flexibly shifting the focus of attention according to context Working Memory: Retaining and applying rules and information over a set period of time Adults
Complex Attention Tasks: Efficiently allocating attentional resources when visual and auditory stimuli are presented together Sustained Attention: Maintaining concentration even in repetitive situations Inhibitory Control Tasks: Suppressing unnecessary responses and selecting the target response Cognitive Processing Speed: Response speed and accuracy related to focused attention Assessment Overview Duration: Approximately 40–60 minutes Method: Computer-based visual and auditory stimulus tasks Age Range: Ages 4 through adults
summary: The CAT (Comprehensive Attention Test) is a standardized assessment that measures multiple sub-domains of attention in a multidimensional way, taking into account developmental characteristics and situational context across age groups. Beyond simply determining whether someone “focuses well or poorly,” it provides objective scores for selective attention, sustained attention, divided attention, working memory, and inhibitory control.
title: Comprehensive Attention Test (CAT)

What is Computer-Based Training (CBT)? Computer-Based Training (CBT) is a program that systematically trains specific cognitive abilities — including attention, memory, executive function, and processing speed — using digital devices such as computers, tablets, and smartphones.
Just as physical exercise improves fitness through repeated use of the body, CBT is grounded in the theory of neuroplasticity: the idea that cognitive abilities can be maintained or improved through deliberate and structured use of the brain.
At ConnectedMind Cognitive Science Institute, we use CBT programs and visual-perceptual training tools to deliver individually tailored cognitive training.
Training Principles Difficulty automatically adjusts to the individual’s cognitive level Trains multiple cognitive domains: attention, working memory, processing speed, executive function Performance is quantitatively recorded to track training progress Structured protocol for systematic cognitive rehabilitation Applications ADHD and learning difficulties Cognitive function decline Need for improved processing speed and working memory Children and adults seeking focused attention training
summary: What is Computer-Based Training (CBT)? Computer-Based Training (CBT) is a program that systematically trains specific cognitive abilities — including attention, memory, executive function, and processing speed — using digital devices such as computers, tablets, and smartphones.
title: Computer-Based Training (CBT)

What is ConnectedMind Cognitive Profiling? ConnectedMind Cognitive Profiling is not simply a test to determine whether there is a “problem” or not. It is a process of comprehensively understanding a person’s cognitive strengths and vulnerabilities, emotional state, and neurophysiological patterns to design an optimized training plan for the individual.
From developmental challenges in children and adolescents to burnout, sleep problems, social anxiety, and reduced focus in adults — regardless of age, we help you deeply understand who you are today and explore the path forward together.

content:
What is the Eye Movement Based Reading Assessment? The Eye Movement Based Reading Assessment uses eye-tracking technology to measure and analyze eye movements in real time while reading. Beyond simply scoring reading performance, it measures fixation count, fixation duration, regression count, binocular coordination, reading speed, and blink patterns to provide objective data on an individual’s reading habits and cognitive strengths and weaknesses.
Based on this data, reading level is compared against age-group norms, helping to accurately diagnose the underlying causes of reading difficulties. It also enables the design of an optimized, personalized training program and the development of effective reading strategies.
Understanding Cognitive Processes Through Eye Movement Analysis Reading is not merely the act of scanning text with the eyes — it is an activity in which complex cognitive processes occur simultaneously. As we read, our eyes move in consistent patterns, and these eye movements directly reflect the brain’s activity in comprehending and processing text.
The Relationship Between Eye Movements and Cognitive Processing When reading, eye movements fall into two main categories:
Fixation: The moment the eye pauses and focuses on a word. During this brief interval, the brain recognizes the text and extracts meaning. When reading speed is slow or comprehension is poor, fixation duration increases and fixation count rises.
Saccade: The rapid movement of the eye from one word to the next. Unlike fixations, saccades do not involve recognition of text meaning. When reading difficulties are present, saccades may be irregular in size, and regressive saccades — backward movements — occur more frequently.
By analyzing eye movement patterns — fixation duration, saccade count, and regression frequency — it is possible to identify not only surface-level reading problems (speed, accuracy) but also the underlying cognitive causes (attention, working memory, visual-perceptual processing).
summary: What is the Eye Movement Based Reading Assessment? The Eye Movement Based Reading Assessment uses eye-tracking technology to measure and analyze eye movements in real time while reading. Beyond simply scoring reading performance, it measures fixation count, fixation duration, regression count, binocular coordination, reading speed, and blink patterns to provide objective data on an individual’s reading habits and cognitive strengths and weaknesses.
title: Eye Movement Based Reading Assessment

content:
Purpose of the Brain Function Assessment Neurofeedback training is a scientifically grounded method that enhances the brain’s self-regulation capacity through its electrical activity. A preliminary brain function assessment is conducted to objectively understand the brain’s current functional state. This allows us to identify areas requiring training and to develop a personalized training plan aligned with the individual’s goals — whether focus, emotional regulation, sleep, stress, or other concerns.
Why a Brain Function Assessment Is Needed Brainwaves are closely related to psychological and physical states. Attention deficits, hyperactivity, anxiety, depression, sleep disorders, chronic stress, and emotional dysregulation can each be associated with patterns of over- or under-activation in specific brain regions. By directly measuring brainwave patterns, we design training grounded in neurological evidence.
How the Assessment Is Conducted The EEG assessment examines the function of each brain region according to the 10–20 international system. Sensors are attached to the scalp to measure the brain’s electrical activity in a resting state. The assessment typically includes recordings with eyes closed (resting EEG) and eyes open (alert EEG). There is no pain or stimulation during the assessment, and children can take it comfortably.

content:
Frequently Asked Questions Q. What happens during the first visit? The first visit begins with an initial consultation and cognitive profiling session. Over approximately 2.5 to 3 hours, you will complete a personalized battery of assessments to identify your current state and goals, after which a tailored training plan is designed together. Regular training sessions follow from there.
Q. How many sessions are needed? It depends on individual goals and initial assessment results, but a minimum of 20–40 sessions is generally recommended. Changes in brain and autonomic nervous system function occur gradually through repeated training, and progress is monitored through periodic assessments.
Q. When do the effects become noticeable? Individual results vary, but many people begin to notice improvements in focus, sleep quality, and emotional regulation around sessions 10–15. Brain training works like muscle training — consistent repetition is key.
Q. Can children participate? Yes, absolutely. Training is available for children aged 5 and above, with protocols adapted to each child’s age and developmental level. A parent or guardian consultation and initial assessment are conducted before training begins to confirm suitability.
Q. Can adults participate? Yes, adults are welcome. We offer personalized training for a wide range of adult concerns, including burnout, sleep difficulties, social anxiety, reduced concentration, and stress regulation.
Q. Can training be combined with medication? Yes, it can. Neurofeedback and cognitive training are non-invasive and are not intended to replace medication, but rather to complement it. We recommend consulting with your physician before beginning training.
Q. Are there any side effects? Neurofeedback, biofeedback, and cognitive training are non-invasive and drug-free, making them generally safe. A small number of individuals may experience temporary fatigue or mild headache during the first few sessions, which typically resolves within 1–2 days. tVNS uses very low current levels and is virtually painless. Please inform us in advance if you have epilepsy, a cardiac pacemaker, or any other specific medical condition.
